Chapter 6: Navigating Daily Life Without the Myth of Free Will.
Waking up to the idea that free will is just an illusion… it’s a bit like stepping into a completely new world, isn’t it? You don’t just flip a switch and suddenly stop blaming yourself, or letting go of old feelings like resentment or pride. Those things tend to stick around, pulling at your attention in all sorts of little ways. But as you move through your days, something interesting starts to happen—small shifts begin to take root almost without you noticing.
Imagine you’re standing on a packed subway, surrounded and jostled by strangers, already running late for work. That familiar spark of irritation rises—why can’t people just be a little more considerate? Maybe in the past, you would’ve rolled your eyes, or even shot a sharp look at someone. But now, you pause. You start to realize that everyone on that train is shaped by their own hidden story—a rough night’s sleep, a sick child at home, maybe a recent job loss. Your frustration softens. Instead of silent judgment, there’s a quiet, almost surprising sense of understanding.
You’ll notice the same thing at home, too, though sometimes it’s more subtle. Maybe your partner forgets an important date. Maybe your kid refuses to do their homework. Or maybe that neighbor’s dog just won’t stop barking late into the night. It’s easy—so easy—to blame, to think, “They could just make a better choice.” But with this new outlook, you find yourself wondering: what led up to this moment? What kind of pressures or habits or past experiences might be shaping their actions?
This isn’t about letting go of boundaries or just becoming a doormat. It’s really about responding with a bit more clarity and kindness. Let’s say a friend cancels plans at the last minute. Sure, you’re disappointed. But instead of stewing in resentment, you might find yourself asking, “I wonder what’s happening for them right now?” The whole conversation shifts—from accusation to real connection.
And when it comes to your own struggles—say, with procrastination, or anxiety—the change is even more noticeable. Instead of seeing these patterns as proof of some personal failing, you start to get curious. What habits or fears or beliefs are actually behind this? And how could you gently understand them, maybe even change them, over time?
Most of us don’t realize how much energy gets spent on blame—whether it’s blaming ourselves or others. Letting go of the myth of free will doesn’t magically erase frustration or disappointment. But it does open up space for living with a little more honesty, and a lot more compassion. Suddenly, life becomes less about assigning fault, and much more about understanding what’s really going on beneath the surface.
